content: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist and immunosuppressant that has demonstrated efficacy in treating various inflammatory conditions, including Crohn's disease. Ulcerative colitis, a related chronic inflammatory bowel disease, presents significant treatment challenges. This systematic review evaluates the current evidence regarding the use of methotrexate for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis. The primary objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of methotrexate in maintaining remission in patients with ulcerative colitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and the Cochrane IBD/FBD group specialized trials register, covering studies up to June 26, 2014. Additional sources, such as references from relevant studies and abstracts from major gastroenterological conferences, were also reviewed to identify unpublished or abstract-only research. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials comparing methotrexate to either placebo or an active comparator in patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two authors. The primary outcome was the rate of clinical or endoscopic relapse, as defined by the individual studies. Secondary outcomes included the frequency and nature of adverse events, changes in disease activity scores, and the steroid-sparing effect of methotrexate. Risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE criteria. Three trials, involving a total of 165 patients, met the inclusion criteria. One study compared oral methotrexate at a dose of 12.5 mg/week to placebo. Another trial compared oral methotrexate at 15 mg/week to either 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP, 1.5 mg/kg/day) or 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA, 3 g/day). The third study evaluated methotrexate at 15 mg/week in combination with sulfasalazine (3 g/day) versus sulfasalazine alone. The placebo-controlled study was deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the study comparing methotrexate to 6-MP and 5-ASA was rated as having a high risk of bias. The trial assessing methotrexate combined with sulfasalazine was rated as having an unclear risk of bias due to uncertainties in sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding. In the placebo-controlled study, no statistically significant difference was observed in the proportion of patients maintaining remission. At nine months, 36% (5/14) of patients receiving methotrexate maintained remission compared to 54% (10/18) of those receiving placebo (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.45). The GRADE analysis rated the quality of evidence for this outcome as low due to the small number of events (15 total). The study comparing methotrexate combined with sulfasalazine to sulfasalazine alone also found no statistically significant difference in remission rates. At 12 months, 100% (14/14) of patients in the combination group maintained remission compared to 75% (9/12) in the sulfasalazine group (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.86). The GRADE analysis rated the quality of evidence for this outcome as very low due to sparse data (23 events) and an unclear risk of bias. Similarly, no significant differences in remission rates were observed between methotrexate and 6-MP or between methotrexate and 5-ASA. At 76 weeks, 14% (1/7) of patients receiving methotrexate maintained remission compared to 64% (7/11) of those receiving 6-MP (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.45). None of the two patients receiving 5-ASA maintained remission (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.06 to 20.71). The GRADE analysis rated the quality of evidence from this study as very low due to high risk of bias and limited data. Adverse events reported across the studies included transient leukopenia, migraine, nausea, dyspepsia, mild alopecia, mild elevations in aspartate aminotransferase levels, peritoneal abscess, hypoalbuminemia, severe rash, and atypical pneumonia. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of methotrexate compared to placebo, sulfasalazine, 6-mercaptopurine, or 5-aminosalicylic acid for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis is inconclusive. The potential benefits of higher doses or parenteral administration of methotrexate remain unknown. Currently, there is no robust evidence to support the use of methotrexate for maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis. Further research, including large-scale, methodologically rigorous randomized controlled trials, is necessary. These studies should explore higher doses of methotrexate (e.g., 15 to 25 mg/week) and parenteral administration to better evaluate its efficacy and safety in this patient population.
